text:
History happened once. The future could go thousands of ways. So I simulated ten thousand of them.

For each one, I built a new twenty-year future by stitching together random three-year blocks of real euro returns from 2000 to 2025.

Keeping three years together preserves how crashes and recoveries tend to follow each other. Then I put in ten thousand euros, and let it run.

Here's the result. The typical future ends with about thirty-two thousand euros after twenty years.

A bad one, the worst five percent, ends with about seven thousand. A great one, the best five percent, more than one hundred and eight thousand.

How to read this: the green line is the middle future, half ended above it and half below. The dark band holds the middle half of all futures, and the light band ninety percent of them.

The spread is the point. Same index, same fees, same discipline, and the result after twenty years ranges from losing a third to more than ten times your money.

How many futures were still below ten thousand euros? After one year, about a third.

After five years, twenty-eight percent. After ten, eighteen. After twenty, still one in ten.

Now the question this video is really about. What if your future starts with a dot-com crash?

So I ran ten thousand more futures, but forced the first three years to be 2000, 2001 and 2002.

Now the typical future ends with only fifteen thousand three hundred euros after twenty years. Half as much.

The typical crash-start future needed eleven years just to get back to ten thousand euros.

Another way to see it: in normal futures, your money had doubled within ten years in forty-four percent of cases. After a crash start, almost never. Zero point two percent.

Give it twenty years, and the gap narrows. Seventy percent of normal futures had doubled by then, and thirty-five percent of the crash-start ones.

Only forty-eight percent were back within ten years. And in one in five, about twenty percent, the money never recovered within twenty years.

One caveat. These futures are built only from the last twenty-six years, which included two of the worst crashes in a century. They might not look like the next twenty.

But the message is clear. If a bubble pops right after you invest a lump sum, time fixes it for most people. Not for everyone, and not quickly.

And for a monthly saver? I ran the same twenty years with three hundred euros a month instead of a lump sum. Seventy-two thousand euros put in.

In normal futures, the typical result was about one hundred and forty-five thousand. In futures that start with the dot-com crash, about one hundred and thirty thousand.

And the chance of ending twenty years of saving with less than you put in? About eleven percent in normal futures. Fourteen percent after a crash start.

Even the unlucky ones weren't wiped out. The worst five percent of crash-start plans still ended with about fifty-two thousand euros, against seventy-two thousand put in.

A crash at the start cut the lump sum's typical result in half. For the monthly saver, it cost about ten percent. Buying through the crash did most of the repair work.
